quiz.q: What happens to a fenced code block inside a `///` doc comment when you run `cargo test`?
options: Nothing, it's purely documentation
It's spell-checked but not compiled
It's compiled and executed as its own test
It's only checked when you run `cargo doc`
quiz.explain: A bare ` ``` ` block inside a doc comment defaults to Rust and is compiled AND run by `cargo test` — a wrong example fails the build, not just the docs.

quiz.q: Why can a doc-test only call `pub` items of the crate it documents?
options: rustdoc doesn't support private items in any context
The example is compiled as if it were external code depending on the crate, the same restriction integration tests have
Because doc-tests run before compilation finishes
It's an arbitrary rustdoc limitation with no deeper reason
quiz.explain: Doc-tests are compiled as standalone programs calling into your crate from the outside, so — like `tests/` integration tests — they only see the public API.

quiz.q: What does prefixing a doc-test line with `# ` (hash, space) do?
options: Comments the line out so it's never compiled
Marks the line as a TODO
Compiles and runs the line, but hides it from the rendered documentation
Turns the line into a doc-test title
quiz.explain: `# `-prefixed lines are still compiled and executed by `cargo test`, they just don't appear in the example a reader sees via `cargo doc`. Handy for hiding setup/imports.

options: The current wall-clock date and time
A monotonic timestamp unaffected by system clock adjustments, meant for measuring elapsed durations
A random benchmark seed
The number of CPU cycles used so far
quiz.explain: `Instant` is designed for measuring elapsed time between two points — it only moves forward, so it isn't thrown off by the system clock being changed.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't you trust a single `Instant::now()` / `.elapsed()` measurement as a real benchmark result?
options: Instant is inaccurate by design
It only measures in whole seconds
A single run is noisy — CPU scaling, other processes, and cold caches can swing it significantly
elapsed() requires unsafe code
quiz.explain: One measurement captures whatever noise happened to be present during that run. It's fine for a rough sanity check, but not for concluding a change made code faster or slower.

quiz.q: Does stable Rust have a built-in `cargo bench`?
options: Yes, identical to `cargo test`
No — the `#[bench]`/`cargo bench` combo is part of the unstable `test` crate, nightly-only
Yes, but only for library crates
No, benchmarking isn't possible in Rust at all
quiz.explain: Built-in benchmarking requires nightly Rust. On stable, the ecosystem standard is the `criterion` crate.

quiz.q: What does `criterion` give you that a single `Instant::elapsed()` timing doesn't?
options: Automatic code optimization
Statistical analysis across many runs, including comparison against the previous run with a confidence interval
A GUI for editing benchmarks
The ability to benchmark without compiling the code
quiz.explain: `criterion` runs your function many times, filters noise statistically, and reports whether a change is a real regression/improvement or just noise — not just a single raw number.

quiz.q: What does wrapping a value in `black_box(...)` prevent in a criterion benchmark?
options: It prevents the value from being printed
It prevents the compiler from optimizing away the computation because it can see the result is unused
It hides the value from the debugger
It slows down the benchmark deliberately for accuracy
quiz.explain: Without `black_box`, the optimizer can notice a computed value is never observably used and delete the whole computation, making the benchmark measure nothing.

flashcards.front: What happens to a fenced code block inside a `///` doc comment when `cargo test` runs?
flashcards.back: It's compiled and executed as its own test — a wrong or stale example fails the build, not just the rendered docs.

flashcards.front: Why can doc-tests only call `pub` items?
flashcards.back: The example is compiled as if it were external code depending on the crate, the same visibility restriction integration tests in `tests/` have.

flashcards.front: What does a `# `-prefixed line inside a doc-test do?
flashcards.back: It's compiled and run like any other line, but hidden from the rendered documentation — used for setup/imports that would clutter the visible example.
Rough, noisy manual timing using std alone — a monotonic timestamp and the Duration since it. Fine for 'is this obviously slow,' not for real comparisons.

flashcards.front: Does stable Rust have a built-in `cargo bench`?
flashcards.back: No — the `#[bench]`/`cargo bench` pair is part of the unstable `test` crate (nightly-only). Stable Rust uses the `criterion` crate instead.

flashcards.front: What makes `criterion` more trustworthy than a single `Instant` measurement?
flashcards.back: It runs the function many times, applies statistical analysis to filter noise, and compares each run to the previous one with a confidence interval.

flashcards.front: What does `black_box` do in a criterion benchmark, and why is it needed?
flashcards.back: It stops the compiler from optimizing away a computation whose result is never observably used — without it you might benchmark nothing at all.

flashcards.front: How is a `benches/*.rs` criterion file structured, and what does `criterion_main!` do?
flashcards.back: It's its own compiled binary (set via `[[bench]] harness = false` in Cargo.toml); `criterion_group!`/`criterion_main!` generate the `fn main` that runs the registered benchmarks.
